title: Bosonic Encodings for Hermite-Galerkin Discretizations of High-Dimensional PDEs and Bayesian Inverse Problems
abstract: The Koopman-von Neumann framework has been proposed to design quantum algorithms for non-linear dynamics. It maps a non-linear ordinary differential equation to a linear partial differential equation (PDE) governing a probability amplitude. Previous works represents this amplitude in the Hermite-function basis, equivalently as a bosonic state, and truncates the total Hermite degree to obtain a representation over $Θ(m\log N)$ qubits, where $N$ is the number of variables and $m$ the truncation order. We extend this approach to a broader class of linear PDEs whose differential operators have a structured polynomial form. We prove convergence of the truncation for both time-dependent dynamics and gapped ground-state problems under explicit regularity and stability assumptions. We then introduce a qubit encoding that supports efficient block encodings of the truncated operators. Finally, we apply the framework to Bayesian inverse problems with Gaussian priors and observation noise, reducing posterior-state preparation to the preparation of a structured Hamiltonian's ground state.
summary: This paper develops a quantum algorithm framework to solve high-dimensional PDEs and Bayesian inverse problems by mapping the dynamics onto a linear system solvable via the Hermite basis. It achieves a space-efficient qubit encoding scaling as $O(m \log N)$ and proves convergence for the approximation, making complex physical inference problems tractable on quantum hardware.
main_problem: The paper addresses the challenge of designing quantum algorithms to solve high-dimensional Partial Differential Equations (PDEs) and Bayesian Inverse Problems.
main_result: It establishes a framework that efficiently encodes the dynamics and posterior state preparation using a qubit representation scaling as $O(m \log N)$ qubits, and proves convergence theorems for the truncation.
method: The core method involves mapping non-linear dynamics to linear PDEs, expanding solutions in the Hermite function basis (Galerkin), and implementing the resulting operators using structured block encodings on qubits.
model_or_system: The system involves high-dimensional probability amplitudes governed by linear PDEs (like Fokker-Planck equations) or the posterior distribution in Bayesian inference. The dynamics are discretized by truncating the Hermite expansion to a finite degree $m$.
key_observables: The total Hermite degree ($m$), the reduced Hermite matrix ($\Gamma^{(j)}$), and the effective Hamiltonian ($H$ or $H_y$) governing the state evolution.
important_parameters: The truncation order $m$ and the number of variables $N$ dictate the qubit scaling $O(m \log N)$. Convergence depends on regularity and stability assumptions.
main_assumptions: Convergence proofs require explicit regularity and stability assumptions on the underlying PDEs and dynamics. The efficient encoding relies on the structured polynomial form of the differential operators.
paper_structure: The paper progresses from establishing the mathematical framework (Koopman-von Neumann, Hermite basis, global truncation) to proving convergence theorems for both time-dependent and ground-state problems. It then details the efficient qubit encoding of the resulting structured operators and applies this machinery to solve Bayesian inverse problems by mapping them to ground-state preparation.
why_interesting: This work provides a concrete, scalable quantum computational pathway for solving complex, high-dimensional physical problems (like those encountered in quantum field theory or statistical physics) by leveraging bosonic encoding techniques.
